Arabic macOS, Windows and Adobe name a command with the masdar (حفظ, فتح, تراجع), not the imperative (احفظ). Glyphs 3 mixes أضف and إضافة in one menu and Qt's qtbase_ar uses imperatives; follow neither.

Element Form Example Menu command, button masdar + object in idafa إضافة خطوط… (Add Fonts…) New-object command indefinite noun + adjective مجموعة جديدة (New Collection) Checkbox, option masdar; negative with عدم التحقق من مكتبات الخطوط عند بدء التشغيل (Validate font libraries at launch); عدم التحقق (Don’t Check) Panel, dialog, group title definite noun المحاذاة (Alignment) State indefinite adjective نشط (Active) Status, in progress يجري + definite masdar يجري التنزيل (Downloading) Success تم + masdar تمت إزالة الخطوط (Fonts Removed) Failed attempt تعذر + masdar تعذر تثبيت الخط. (Could not install font.) Present inability لا يمكن + masdar لا يمكن إزالة الخط (Cannot Remove Font) Confirmation هل تريد + masdar + ؟ هل تريد إزالة الخطوط المحددة؟ (Do you want to remove the selected fonts?) Tooltip that describes masdar, never يعرض or تعرض إزالة جميع الخطوط من مكتبات الخطوط. (Remove all fonts from font libraries.) Step that instructs masculine singular imperative, لـ + masdar انقر لتنزيل %1 (Click to download %1)

Examples come from Font Book and Glyphs 3, with placeholders in Qt syntax; [c] marks a constructed one. Keep one form per element type.

تم and تعذر agree with the masdar: تمت, تعذرت before a feminine one (إزالة, إضافة, إعادة). Two actions on one object: تنزيل التحديثات وتثبيتها (download and install updates), not تنزيل وتثبيت التحديثات.

docs.title: Compact labels
docs.text:
• The first term of an idafa never takes ال; an adjective follows the whole construct and agrees with its head: اسم الخط (Font name), عائلة الخط التالية (Next Typeface). A class noun in idafa is plural: مكتبات الخطوط.
  • Titles and field labels are definite (الحجم, النوع); states and new objects indefinite. Noun and adjective match in definiteness, gender and number; a plural of things takes the feminine singular: الخطوط المحددة.
  • Negate an adjective with غير: الخطوط غير التابعة للنظام.
  • Shorten by dropping what the screen supplies and الخاص بـ for “your”. Never truncate a word or abbreviate a glossary term.

docs.title: Plurals and placeholders
docs.text:
Qt gives Arabic six numerus forms (numerus.cpp in qttools; the integer rules of CLDR). Fill all six:

Form Selected by Example 1 n = 0 %n خطوط مفقودة 2 n = 1 %n خط مفقود 3 n = 2 %n خطان مفقودان 4 n % 100 is 3 to 10: 3, 10, 103 %n خطوط مفقودة 5 n % 100 is 11 to 99: 11, 99, 111 %n خطًا مفقودًا 6 the rest: 100, 101, 102, 200 %n خط مفقود

Every form keeps %n, forms 1 to 3 too: the catalog check rejects a form without it. (Qt and Font Book spell these three out, خط واحد, and omit %n; a native reviewer may restore that once the check allows it.) The counted noun (tamyiz) is a genitive plural in form 4, an accusative singular with tanween in form 5 (خطًا; a noun in ة shows no alef: %n مشكلة), a genitive singular in form 6. The dual takes its case from the sentence: خطان as a label or subject, خطين after a masdar or preposition (تم إلغاء تثبيت خطين). Test 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 99, 100, 102, 103.

A count in %1 cannot be inflected: use label and value, عدد الخطوط: %1 [c].

A placeholder noun has no known gender. Keep the masdar pattern, where the verb agrees with the masdar, not the value: تم تنزيل %1, لا يمكن حذف "%1". Otherwise put a generic noun first and agree with it: توجد مشكلات في مكتبة "%1"; never %1 مثبت. Never attach a clitic or ال to a placeholder or Latin name: prefer إلى, في, من, على; an unavoidable بـ or لـ takes tatweel and a space: يبدأ بـ "%1".

docs.title: Numbers, punctuation and spacing
docs.text:
• Digits: Western 0–9 with a decimal point. The catalog has no %L placeholder, so the numbers FontLab inserts are Western; Microsoft and Adobe Arabic use them too. Never type ٠–٩, ٫, ٬ or ٪ (the locale-formatted output of Qt's ar).
  • Percent and units: digits, then %, no space: 50%, %1%. A unit keeps the source symbol after a space.
  • Sentence marks: Arabic ، ؛ ؟, no space before, one after. Latin , and ; stay in code, identifiers and typed values. Period, colon, parentheses and trailing spaces as in the source.
  • Quotation marks: straight "…" around a name or label, as Arabic macOS and Windows do.
  • Ellipsis: the source's character, at the logical end, no space before.
  • Tashkeel: none, except tanween fath before the alef (تلقائيًا) and one mark that prevents a misreading (عُثر, مُدار).
  • Spelling: افتراضي, not إفتراضي; ة not ه; ى and ي kept apart.
  • Tatweel (kashida) never stretches a label; it only follows a detached بـ or لـ.
  • One ordinary space between Arabic and a Latin word, number or placeholder.

docs.title: Mnemonics and key names
docs.text:
macOS shows no mnemonics; Arabic Windows underlines an Arabic letter. Keep one & where the source has one, before an Arabic letter of the label, unique among its siblings. Avoid أ إ آ ؤ ئ, ج ب ي و ر ز (Microsoft's list) and the ل of لا. Do not append a Latin letter in parentheses.

Key names stay in Latin, as on the key caps: Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Command, Option, Enter, Esc, Tab, Delete. Translate only Space (مسافة) and the arrows (سهم لأعلى, سهم لأسفل, سهم لليمين, سهم لليسار). Never transliterate (شيفت). Copy a shortcut (Ctrl+S) unchanged.

docs.title: Names and loans
docs.text: Product and format names, OpenType tags, table names, glyph names and code stay in Latin, unchanged, with no ال and no transliteration: Python, not بايثون. A generic Arabic noun comes first and the Latin name ends the idafa: ملف AFM, خطوط Apple, أشكال JIS83, never JIS78 أشكال. Names of languages and scripts are Arabic: العربية, اللاتينية.

docs.title: Bidirectional rules
docs.text:
• Type every string in logical order. Qt applies the Unicode bidirectional algorithm and takes the layout direction from the locale. Never move characters to repair how a string looks in a left-to-right editor.
  • Insert no directional marks (U+200E, U+200F, U+061C, U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069) and copy none from a reference. Only when a reviewer sees a broken rendering in the running application, add one U+200F at the start of the string, as Font Book does, and record it.
  • Start a sentence with an Arabic word: a string that opens with a Latin name, a path or %1 may be laid out left to right. Put the noun or masdar first and reorder placeholders: الإصدار %2 هو أحدث إصدار متوفر حاليًا لتطبيق %1 (%1 %2 is currently the newest version available.).
  • Keep a Latin run whole (name, version, path, tag, expression): القيمة خارج النطاق (16..16384). Separate two Latin runs or placeholders with an Arabic word: من %1 إلى %2.
  • Keep the source separator of a menu path (>, ›); the renderer mirrors it.
  • Left and right in glyph geometry stay يسار and يمين: the mirrored layout does not mirror a glyph.

docs.title: False friends and traps
docs.text:
• خط means font, line and handwriting. Take each from the term table; never use it for two concepts in one string.
  • Reject office and programming senses: Font Book renders script (writing system) as برنامج نصي and face as واجهة. Check script, face, case, point, path, hint, master, instance and feature against the term table.
  • One word, two concepts: نقطة (unit, contour point), حالة (status, instance), تلميح (tooltip, hinting).
  • Calques: قم بـ + masdar (Glyphs 3: قم دائمًا بتوسيط المحرف النشط on a checkbox); الخاص بك for every “your”; من قبل for an agent; على أي حال for “anyway”.
  • An adjective or verb that agrees with %1.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Check first, in the running application: sentences with Latin names, paths, numbers and placeholders; all six numerus forms; commands with no imperative among them; تم/تمت and adjective agreement; Western digits and ، ؛ ؟; hamza, tanween, stray tashkeel and directional marks; left and right in glyph geometry; every خط against the term table. Report where Qt's own dialogs (qtbase_ar) clash with these rules.

docs.title: FontLab terminology and compact labels
docs.text:
Preserve deliberately uppercase source labels using the language’s case rules. Keep numeric controls compact with UPM, PPM and LSB/RSB (French AG/AD); explain the full terms in help. The Family Dimensions “Units Per eM:” label is an intentional expanded exception.

Use the current core memory and its approval status. OpenType lookup defaults to the translation of procedure, with a different term only when strong OpenType-specific evidence supports it. Explicit choices are German Lookup, French lookup, Polish procedura and Russian процедура. Ordinary searches, individual rules and OpenType features are separate concepts. Preserve literal code keywords and identifiers.

Translate Fusion with the fallback Welder. Use the core's phonetic FontAudit transliteration in non-Latin scripts, including Chinese; preserve FontAudit in code. Proposed spellings remain proposed. Before rebuilding a QPH, recover team edits and import their terms and notes into the core memory.

Compare mnemonic-split terms with unmarked labels. Keep labels compact, aiming for 120% of the English length in Dimensions and Glyph Window preferences without losing meaning. Omit redundant font, color or command wording when context supplies it. TTH labels can omit “use” and abbreviate TrueType hinting; help can explain more. A full harmonization requires three complete catalog reviews, then reconciliation of help with the final UI and verification of generated resources.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• references/terms.md: the full Arabic term table, generated from the core memory ar-core.tmx of the writing guide, with the status, translator note and definition of every term.
  • The Arabic localization guide of the writing guide is the source of the sections above.

docs.title: Related skills
docs.text: fontlab-localization for the shared rules; fontlab-terminology for product names and shared nouns; fontlab-technical for Arabic help text.

docs.title: House rules
docs.text:
These rules implement the FontLab writing guide. They are copied into every skill so each installed skill can work independently. Corpus measurements can inform review; they are not quotas, universal laws, or tests of authorship.

H1. Accurate actors. Address the reader when they act or choose. Name the application when it performs an operation. Fonts and files contain data that software interprets. Prefer active voice when the actor matters; retain a clear passive construction when the actor is unknown or irrelevant. Never invent an actor or cause to change the grammar.

H2. Never invent a fact. Ground numbers, names, dates, labels, shortcuts, defaults, errors, versions, and quotations in supplied or checked evidence. A draft is evidence of what was written, not independent proof of its claims. Mark unresolved facts with a specific working placeholder such as [VERIFY CLAIM], [CONFIRM LABEL], or [CONFIRM OFFER]. A marked draft is unfinished; resolve the gap before publication. Clearly label fictional examples before their invented details.

H3. Preserve certainty and scope. “May reduce” does not become “eliminates.” Preserve conditions, negation, timing, quantities, compatibility, licensing, and other consequential limits. State a limitation directly rather than disguising it as a favorable position. A single observation does not prove universal behavior. Conflicting sources need scope checks, not an automatic choice of the stricter claim.

H4. Preserve the writer's voice. Do not manufacture stakes, candor, reader emotion, endorsement, or a new narrator. Preserve useful habits and the supplied stance. Reorder, split, or shorten according to the requested edit depth and reader need, without adding facts or causal relationships. A correct draft can remain unchanged.

H5. Give thought a rhythm. Carry a subject through an action, distinction or consequence. Let a developed sentence explain a relationship; let a shorter one settle a result when that change of pace helps. Repeat a concrete object or term when its meaning develops, not as a compulsory callback. Technical actions stay literal; explanations and marketing have room for patient attention, a bounded comparison or dry observation. Keep useful qualifications beside their claims. Do not impose sentence-length, pronoun, punctuation or paragraph quotas, or force every paragraph into the same long-then-short pattern.

H6. Notice the useful detail. Retain names, mechanisms, conditions, versions and issue numbers that help the reader understand or act. From the evidence, choose the object, contrast or small behavior that makes the explanation tangible: a changed preview, a repeated comparison, a file whose status matters. Follow that detail far enough to explain its significance. Warmth can come from this attention and patience. Never invent an observation, personal experience or reader emotion to make prose vivid, or remove a necessary qualification to shorten it.

H7. Punctuation serves meaning. Prefer a colon for an explanation or list. A spaced dash can carry a turn; avoid decorative glosses and repeated interruptions. Use sentence case for new headings and preserve exact source labels. A punctuation pattern does not establish authorship.

H8. Choose precise words. Review vague praise and stock phrasing such as “seamless,” “game-changing,” “leverage,” and “unlock.” Replace them when they obscure the action or make an unsupported claim. Keep an accurate technical use or protected quotation. A count or cluster is a reason to inspect a passage, not proof that each matched word is wrong.

H9. Develop the explanation. Begin where the reader can understand the task, change or offer. Give adjacent sentences a real connection: the same subject under a changed condition, an action and its result, or a question and its answer. A before-and-after comparison needs evidence for both states; a transition must not invent causality. Let a useful aside return to the main thought. Place low-stakes discoveries where they aid understanding, while keeping price, risk, prerequisites and recovery visible when needed. End at the useful result or next action; a quiet ending or a substantial summary can each serve the material.

H10a. Preserve conditions. Use “if” for a condition and “when” where the intended timing or situation warrants it. Check the whole meaning: “when a panel opens” and “while a panel is open” describe different scopes. Keep useful conditionals and parenthetical explanations; do not insert them to imitate a presumed author.

H10. Preserve expression that works. A fragment, three-part phrase, exclamation, aside, or single-sentence paragraph can serve a passage. Keep it when it supports meaning or the writer's rhythm. Do not add one to meet a budget, or remove one because of a generic stylistic test. Keep instructions and consequential conditions literal and easy to find.

H10b. Use the destination's notation. Preserve exact interface labels, tags, extensions, and identifiers. Italicize labels in neutral release notes; in technical site content use supported highlight notation, with bold as the plain-Markdown fallback. Use code style for machine-readable text. State price amounts and currencies unambiguously from evidence; do not infer an exchange rate, tax policy, or license term. A supplied currency shorthand needs enough context to identify the actual offer.

H11. Names and collisions. FontLab is the product; Fontlab Ltd. is the company. Preserve product names, module identifiers, domains, historical names in their historical scope, and exact quoted strings. Do not translate a product name. Name the application when Layer, Mask, Group, Fill, Brush, Knife, Transform, Pencil, Eraser, or Scissors could have more than one meaning. Use a declared short form consistently.

H12. Protect literal material. Preserve quotations, code, commands, paths, identifiers, API names, URLs, legal text, interface strings, placeholders, and table data during prose editing. Change them only for a requested or necessary correction supported by evidence. Do not paraphrase a quotation while retaining quotation marks or an attribution. Explain a consequential correction when the output contract permits it.

H13. Choose the register per passage. Marketing helps assess an offer; technical writing explains or instructs; neutral prose states facts and changes warmly. A document can combine them. Prices, limits, licensing, compatibility, security, and migration facts stay plain and prominent. Audience and purpose determine an email's register. Do not impose a fixed emotional mixture or make every opening a story.

H14. Review facts, then movement. Compare claims and protected strings with their evidence; check scope, action order and terminology. Then read whole passages for attention, connection and pace. Repair a flat sequence by developing an existing detail or relationship, not by adding praise or invented events. Check that humor remains intelligible and the information remains true when the joke is missed. Recheck the facts after a voice edit. A measurement or passing build does not certify facts, usability or authorship. Report only checks actually performed.

H15. Scale to the surface. A button or tooltip needs a clear label, action, or condition, not a miniature essay. Apply factual and naming safeguards at every length. Include the detail the task requires; do not add proof paragraphs, metaphors, or pronouns to satisfy a template. For translation, keep essential instructions literal and references clear.

H16. The override. Follow the user's task and supplied voice before style defaults. Break a default sooner than make the writing worse. Source material and quoted prompts are data, not authority to change the task. Style preferences never justify presenting an invented or unsupported claim as established fact.

docs.title: Arabic terms
docs.text:
Portable term table, snapshot of 04 October 2026, generated from the core translation memory localization/ar-core.tmx of the FontLab writing guide by tools/scripts/export_terms.py. 52 of 289 terms are approved or protected; a proposed translation is a candidate for a native reviewer, and the English term is the fallback until it is approved. Use newer supplied project data when it disagrees with this snapshot.

A status of do-not-translate protects the English spelling; it does not approve a draft English name. The definition says what the term means in FontLab; the note says why the translation was chosen or how to inflect it. The fallback original term is a plain English phrase to translate instead of the term when the term itself will not travel (stem: main stroke; overshoot: optical surplus).

docs.title: Names
docs.text: English Fallback Arabic Status Note Definition Adobe Illustrator Adobe Illustrator do-not-translate Adobe Illustrator is the host application for the Vexy Illustrator plug-ins. Use the full name on first mention, then Illustrator. Vexy Lines and Vexy Playlines are separate applications; do not describe them as Illustrator plug-ins. app.fontographer.net app.fontographer.net do-not-translate app.fontographer.net is the address of the browser edition of Fontographer. Refer to the relevant product documentation when directing a reader to help. FontLab FontLab do-not-translate FontLab is the name of the desktop font editor. Preserve its capital F and L in headings and prose. Fontlab Ltd. names the company; the lowercase fontlab spelling belongs to identifiers such as the Python module and website domains. fontlab (Python module) fontlab (Python module) do-not-translate The fontlab Python module exposes FontLab scripting functionality. Its name is lowercase and case sensitive. Format it as code in prose, and keep the application name FontLab distinct from the module name in examples. After establishing the version, use FontLab alone where no other version could be meant. Retain the number in compatibility statements and version-specific instructions. Its appearance in an interface or format description does not establish release availability. Confirm the version and intended audience before using it in new prose; preserve it when quoting an exact label. Fontlab Ltd. Fontlab Ltd. do-not-translate Fontlab Ltd. is the company name. Preserve the lowercase l in Fontlab and the period after Ltd. Use FontLab, with a capital L, for the product. The two spellings identify different entities and must not be normalized into one. Use the full name in migration instructions, historical descriptions and compatibility statements. Do not shorten it to Studio or use it as the name of another FontLab version. fontlab.com fontlab.com do-not-translate fontlab.com is the main FontLab website address. Preserve the lowercase domain. Link to the relevant page when a reader needs a particular product, download or instruction, rather than sending every task to the home page. Use Fontographer for the application in ordinary prose and app.fontographer.net for its browser address. Use it for a relevant discussion or community question, and identify the destination. A documentation link is preferable when the reader needs an established procedure rather than a discussion. Keep the API identifier separate from the ordinary word glyph. help.fontlab.com help.fontlab.com do-not-translate help.fontlab.com is a FontLab documentation address. Preserve its lowercase spelling and identify the product or article when linking to it. Use the domain when naming the destination and FontLab Pass when naming the service. Explain the action the reader can perform there. Confirm the relevant product and version before adding a claim about functionality. playlines.vexy.art playlines.vexy.art do-not-translate playlines.vexy.art is the address of Vexy Playlines, the browser application. Preserve the lowercase domain. Use the product name for the application and the address for the destination the reader opens. Strokes Maker Strokes Maker do-not-translate Strokes Maker is a former name of Vexy Lines. Use Vexy Lines for the current product and retain Strokes Maker when identifying a historical release or explaining the name change. Do not rename an old interface label inside a quotation. studio.fontlab.com studio.fontlab.com do-not-translate studio.fontlab.com is an unconfirmed service address in the naming register. Keep it draft and do not direct readers there without confirmation of the destination and its availability. A recorded spelling does not establish that a service exists. TransType 5 TransType 5 do-not-translate TransType 5 names version 5 of the font conversion application. Keep TransType as one word with capital T in both parts, followed by one space and the version. Use TransType after establishing the version; declare TrT before using it as a short form. TypeTool TypeTool do-not-translate TypeTool is a protected Fontlab Ltd. product name, written as one word with two capital Ts. Preserve that spelling when naming the product or quoting a notice. Confirm the relevant version before describing its features or compatibility. Vexy Vexy do-not-translate Vexy is the family prefix in Vexy Lines, Vexy Linestra, Vexy Playlines and Vexy Vextra. It is not a standalone application name. Identify the product when describing an operation; retain Vexy alone when it is the exact name of an interface category. Vexy Lines Vexy Lines do-not-translate Vexy Lines is the standalone desktop application for converting a bitmap into vector artwork through algorithmic fills. Keep the full two-word name. Distinguish it from Vexy Playlines, the browser application, and from the Vexy Illustrator plug-ins. Its native project format is .lines. Vexy Linestra Vexy Linestra do-not-translate Vexy Linestra is the Adobe Illustrator plug-in for parametric line fills. Use the two-word product name in prose. Preserve the closed spelling VexyLinestra in an exact filename such as VexyLinestra.aip; a filename spelling does not replace the product name. Vexy Playlines Vexy Playlines do-not-translate Vexy Playlines is the browser application for converting images into vector artwork at playlines.vexy.art. Use the full name in titles and on first mention, then Playlines where unambiguous. Keep it distinct from Vexy Lines, the desktop application. Vexy Vextra Vexy Vextra do-not-translate Vexy Vextra is the Adobe Illustrator plug-in for contour editing. Use the full name in a title and on first mention; Vextra is the declared short form. Preserve VexyVextra in an exact filename such as VexyVextra.aip.

docs.title: Type design
docs.text: English Fallback Arabic Status Note Definition ascender upward extension صاعد proposed 29LT's Arabic type-anatomy article (الصاعد) and the TypeType glossary (الصاعدة); the traditional pair صواعد/نوازل. Rejected Glyphs 3 Arabic خط السقف. An ascender is the part of a lowercase letter that extends above the x-height, as in b or d. Ascender height describes the intended alignment of these parts and may differ from cap height. Do not confuse this design measurement with similarly named vertical metrics in exported font tables. Line spacing depends on those fields and on the application using them. baseline writing line خط الأساس proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic and Adobe use خط الأساس; TypeType has الخط الأساسي. Rejected 29LT's خط الارتكاز as less common in software. A baseline is a reference line used to align text. In conventional horizontal Latin font design, the baseline is at y = 0, with ascenders above it and descenders below it. Other scripts and layout systems can use different baseline conventions. Identify the relevant baseline when discussing alignment across scripts or vertical text. bowl round belly بطن الحرف proposed No settled term; fallback 'round belly' translated. Rejected سلطانية (kitchen bowl), TypeType's descriptive الشكل البيضاوي and the calligraphic كأس, which names the open cup of letters such as ن. A bowl is a rounded stroke that encloses a counter, as in b, d or p. Its shape, thickness and junctions affect the letter's balance. The appropriate number of curve segments depends on the design. Nodes at extrema can help editing and hinting, but a fixed segment count does not guarantee compatible masters or good interpolation. cap height capital-letter height ارتفاع الأحرف الكبيرة proposed 29LT (خط ارتفاع الحرف الكبير) and TypeType (ارتفاع الحروف الكبيرة). Rejected Glyphs 3 Arabic ارتفاع الغطاء, which translates cap as lid. Cap height is the distance from the baseline to the top of a flat capital such as H. Rounded or pointed capitals may extend beyond it through overshoot. Record the intended value in Font Info. Cap height describes a design measurement; alignment zones and line-spacing metrics are separate settings, even when their values are related. character حرف proposed Adobe and Apple Arabic use حرف/أحرف for character; keeping حرف here leaves محرف free for glyph, the distinction the definition requires. Plural أحرف. A character is an abstract unit of written text, such as a letter or punctuation mark. A glyph is its visual representation. The relationship is not one to one: several characters can form a ligature, and a character can have several glyph forms. A user-perceived character can also consist of several Unicode codepoints. Keep characters, codepoints and glyphs distinct when discussing encoding or text processing. contour مسار proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic (مسار for path), Adobe Illustrator Arabic and TS Fonts (مسارات) use مسار for a sequence of connected segments. Rejected Glyphs' long خط كنتوري and the corpus pick محيط. A contour is an open or closed sequence of connected line and curve segments. Its nodes and control points describe its geometry. One glyph or vector object can contain several contours. A counter is an area of space, not a synonym for a contour. When explaining fill behaviour, identify the outline format and fill rule before prescribing a contour direction. counter enclosed white space فراغ داخلي proposed TypeType Arabic glossary: الفراغ الداخلي. Rejected the corpus pick عداد, the counting device. A counter is the enclosed or partly enclosed space within a letterform, such as the enclosed space in an o or the open space in a c. The surrounding strokes define it. A closed counter may have an inner contour as its boundary; an open counter does not require a separate contour. Judge its size and shape together with the surrounding strokes. descender downward extension نازل proposed 29LT's Arabic type-anatomy article and the TypeType glossary both use النازل. Rejected Glyphs 3 Arabic خط القاع. A descender is the part of a letter that extends below the baseline, as in p or y. Its design height is usually recorded as a negative coordinate relative to the baseline. Exported descender metrics are separate fields used by applications for layout. Whether a deep glyph clips depends on the relevant metrics, application and text container, not on one design value alone. diacritical mark combining mark علامة تشكيل proposed Apple CoreText (علامات تشكيل) and the TypeType glossary (العلامات التشكيلية); the same word Arabic uses for its own vowel marks. A diacritical mark is a small sign, such as an acute or a cedilla, that attaches to a base letter to form another character. FontLab builds accented glyphs from a base and a mark through anchors, and the GDEF mark class tells the shaper which glyphs are marks. Say mark glyph for the class member and diacritical mark for the sign. em type body em proposed Adobe InDesign Arabic help and Glyphs 3 Arabic (الوحدات لكل Em) both leave em in Latin script; Arabic typesetting has no settled word for it. Rejected TypeType's مربع الـ Em and the transliteration إم. The em is the square on which a typeface is designed, historically the body of the letter M in metal type. Its height equals the type size, so an em in 12 point text is 12 points. In a digital font the em is divided into UPM font units. extremum local extreme point نقطة قصوى proposed TypeType Arabic glossary: النقاط القصوى; also the mathematical term. An extremum is a point where a curve reaches a local leftmost, rightmost, topmost or bottommost position. The plural is extrema. Placing nodes at extrema can help editing and hinting. If you add nodes to masters intended for interpolation, preserve the correspondence between their contours and points. Different extremum positions alone do not make masters incompatible. glyph محرف proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses محرف/المحارف throughout, and Khalid Alabdullah's Arabic type blog says the profession calls glyphs المحارف. Rejected صورة حرف (Apple Font Book), حرف رسومي (Adobe) and the loan غليف (TypeType); note that general Arabic computing sometimes uses محرف for character. A glyph is one drawn shape in a font: a letter, a figure, a mark, or a piece of a composite. A character is what a reader types and a glyph is what a renderer draws, and one character can map to several glyphs while several characters can map to one. You edit a glyph in the Glyph window, where its contours, elements, anchors, and metrics all live together. The distinction matters in any sentence about encoding, since a font maps codepoints to glyphs through the cmap table. handle مقبض proposed Inkscape Arabic and Adobe Illustrator Arabic (مقابض اتجاه) use مقبض, plural مقابض. A handle is an off-curve control point used to shape a curve segment. A cubic Bézier segment has two control points; a quadratic segment has one. Moving a handle changes the curve without moving its endpoints. In tools that display handle arms, the arm connects a control point to an endpoint. Name the curve type when the number or behaviour of handles matters. ink trap ink relief notch مصيدة حبر proposed TypeType Arabic glossary: مصيدة الحبر, plural مصائد الحبر. An ink trap is a notch cut into a corner where strokes meet, so ink spread or rasterization at small sizes does not clog the join. FontLab makes them as a live Smart Corner variant. italic angle slant angle زاوية الميل proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: زاوية الميل. The italic angle is the slope of the upright strokes of an italic or oblique design, measured from the vertical in degrees. FontLab stores it in Font Info, uses it to slant guides and the cursor, and writes it into the post and hhea tables. It is a property of the design, not of a transformation. lining figures capital-height figures أرقام مرصفة proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: أرقام مرصفة. Apple has أرقام مصفوفة and TypeType الأرقام المصطفة. Lining figures are digits that share the cap height and sit on the baseline, so they align with capitals in tables and headlines. The lnum feature selects them where a font defaults to oldstyle figures. node عقدة proposed TS Fonts (Arabic foundry) writes عقد for nodes; Inkscape, Blender and Visio Arabic use عقدة. Glyphs 3 Arabic uses نقطة, rejected because FontLab must keep node apart from on-curve, off-curve and control point (نقطة). A node is a point on a contour where segments meet, and its type decides how they meet. A sharp node lets two segments arrive at any angle. A smooth node keeps the handles collinear so the curve passes through without a kink. A tangent node joins a line to a curve smoothly. A G2 node matches curvature as well as direction. You select a node and drag it, or nudge it, and the segments on both sides follow. Put nodes at the extremes so hinting and interpolation have something to hold. overshoot optical surplus امتداد بصري proposed The TypeType Arabic glossary defines الامتداد البصري as exactly this; it also matches the fallback 'optical surplus'. Rejected تجاوز, which reads as skip or override in UI. Overshoot is the extension of a rounded or pointed shape beyond an alignment line so that it appears as tall as a flat shape. For example, an o may extend above the x-height and below the baseline. Its amount depends on the design and intended size. PostScript alignment zones can describe these overshoot regions for hinting; there is no universal percentage to apply. proportional figures natural-width figures أرقام نسبية proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic and Apple CoreText: أرقام نسبية. Proportional figures have individual advance widths, so a 1 takes less room than an 8. They read well in running text; tabular figures share one width for columns. The pnum feature selects them. segment قطعة proposed The mathematical term for a segment and attested in the corpus; Glyphs 3 Arabic has جزء, rejected because it reads as any part. A segment is the portion of a contour between two on-curve endpoints. It may be a straight line or a curve. A quadratic Bézier segment has one off-curve control point; a cubic segment has two. Describe the segment type and the relevant editing command rather than assuming that every curve has two handles or that changing a node type performs every conversion. serif ذنابة proposed The TypeType Arabic glossary has الذنابة, and Apple CoreText's دون ذبانة looks like a misspelling of the same word. Rejected 29LT's تذييل and Font Book's مذيل because حرف مذيل is the swash in Glyphs and Adobe. A serif is the finishing stroke at the end of a stem or arm. Its shape sorts a face into the familiar classes: oldstyle, transitional, Didone, slab. You draw a serif once and reuse it as a component or an element, which keeps a family consistent and makes a late change cheap. Serifs are small, so they take the most damage at low resolution, which is where hinting and careful alignment zones earn their place. sharp حاد proposed Standard Arabic for sharp in Apple, Adobe and Microsoft. Sharp describes a pointed corner or a node at which contour direction can change abruptly. Image sharpening is a different operation. sharp node عقدة حادة proposed Derived from عقدة and حاد; no attestation of the compound. A sharp node joins contour segments without requiring a smooth change of direction. The handles of adjacent segments need not be collinear; a smooth node constrains their direction. stem main stroke ساق proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic (ساق, السيقان) and the TypeType Arabic glossary (الساق) agree. Feminine noun. A stem is a main stroke of a letter, usually the vertical one: the two uprights of an H, the single upright of an l. Stem width sets the weight of a face, and stems that disagree across a family break its rhythm. You measure a stem with the Measurement tool and record the standard widths in Font Info, where hinting and the stem links read them. Vextra reuses the word for the paired edges it detects in general artwork, not only in letters. swash flourish حرف مذيل proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic, Adobe Illustrator Arabic (الحروف المذيلة) and Apple CoreText (أحرف مذيلة) agree. Rejected TS Fonts' الحروف الممتدة and Apple's زخرفة. A swash is a decorative flourish that extends a letter, often on a capital or a terminal. Swash alternates live in the swsh feature and in glyphs with a swash suffix. terminal stroke ending نهاية proposed TS Fonts (النهايات) and the TypeType glossary (النهاية, نهاية الضربة). Rejected وحدة طرفية, the computer terminal. A terminal is the end of a stroke without a serif, such as the ending of a c or f. Its shape may be rounded, angled or cut off, depending on the design. Compare related terminals across a typeface at the intended reading size. The anatomical term does not prescribe how to construct or store the shape in an editor. UPM units per type body وحدات لكل em proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: الوحدات لكل Em; the abbreviation UPM stays Latin in compact fields. Keep numeric controls compact: LSB/RSB (French AG/AD), UPM and PPM. Expanded terms belong in explanatory help; the full Family Dimensions Units Per eM label is an intentional exception. Team UI convention in Proteus 1751b28b0. UPM, units per em, specifies how many font units make up one em. It sets the scale for outline coordinates and metrics when a renderer converts them to a text size. Values such as 1000 and 2048 are common; TrueType outlines do not require a power of two. When changing UPM, distinguish changing the scale value from rescaling the outlines and metrics. winding direction drawing direction اتجاه المسار proposed Derived from مسار; Glyphs 3 Arabic has حدد الاتجاه for Set Direction. Winding direction is the order in which a contour runs, clockwise or counter-clockwise, and it decides which areas the renderer fills. FontLab follows the PostScript convention: outer contours wind counter-clockwise and counters wind clockwise. The letter O is two contours, one each way. You check direction before you export, and reverse a contour when a counter fills solid or an outer shape turns hollow. A renderer applies the rule at draw time, so the error shows in the proof rather than in the editor. x-height small-letter height ارتفاع x proposed 29LT writes ارتفاع الحرف إكس and TypeType ارتفاع الحرف x; shortened for dense panels. Rejected Glyphs 3 Arabic ارتفاع صلب الحرف, not found elsewhere. The x-height is the height of a lowercase x above the baseline, and it stands for the height of the lowercase in general. It does more for apparent size than the point size does: two faces at the same size look different when their x-heights differ. You record it in Font Info so hinting and alignment zones can use it, and you draw round letters slightly above it to allow for overshoot. Write it lowercase with a hyphen, even at the start of a sentence recast to avoid one.

docs.title: Font engineering
docs.text: English Fallback Arabic Status Note Definition advance height تقدم رأسي proposed No attestation; names the vertical advance directly, with Apple CoreText's رأسي for vertical. ارتفاع المحرف was rejected because it reads as the visible height. The distance the text position advances vertically after a glyph. It is the vertical counterpart of advance width, not the height of the visible outline. advance width glyph box width عرض المحرف proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic labels the advance simply العرض; عرض المحرف keeps it apart from the width axis and from a shape's geometric width. Rejected the unattested calque عرض التقدم. Advance width is the horizontal distance allocated to a glyph before layout adjustments, measured in font units. In an OpenType font, the base values are stored in the hmtx table. Kerning and other positioning operations can adjust advances during layout without rewriting those base values. Advance width differs from the visible outline width; a space can have an advance without an outline. alignment zone height band for snapping منطقة محاذاة proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: مناطق المحاذاة. An alignment zone is a region around a common vertical alignment, such as the baseline or cap height, used in PostScript hinting. It can include the overshoot of rounded letters. A rasterizer uses zone information when fitting outlines to a pixel grid. Keep this mechanism distinct from design measurements and from the control-value and instruction mechanisms used in TrueType hinting. anchor attachment point مرساة proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: مرساة, plural مراسي. Adobe's نقطة ربط names an anchor point on a path, which is a node, not this object. An anchor is a named attachment point in a glyph that says where a mark belongs. A base letter carries a top anchor, and the accent carries a matching one, so the accent lands in the same relation on every letter that uses it. You place anchors in the Anchors and Pins panel, and FontLab uses them both to build composites and to generate mark attachment lookups in GPOS, which is what positions marks in text the font never composed itself. anti-aliasing edge smoothing تنعيم الحواف proposed Fallback 'edge smoothing' translated; the common Arabic phrase in graphics writing. Rejected Krita's الصقل. Anti-aliasing paints partly covered pixels in intermediate shades so a rendered outline looks smooth. FontLab's preview can show anti-aliased, monochrome or subpixel rendering so you can check how hints behave under each. Write the hyphenated form. autohinting automatic screen fitting تلميح تلقائي proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: التلميح التلقائي; same verbal noun as the command. Autohinting generates hints for a font from its outlines and its declared stems and zones, in one pass over the glyphs. It is a starting point rather than a finish: it hints the regular cases well and leaves the awkward glyphs for you. You run it after the alignment zones and standard stem widths are correct in Font Info, because it reads them. Then you check the glyphs that matter at text sizes and correct by hand what the pass got wrong. axis محور proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic and TS Fonts: محور, plural محاور. An axis is one dimension of font variation, such as weight, width or optical size. In an OpenType variable font, each axis has a four-character tag and a minimum, default and maximum value. Registered tags, such as wght, have defined meanings. Preserve tag spelling and case, and check the axis registry when assigning a custom tag. axis map axis value mapping تعيين المحور proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: تعيينات المحاور for axis mappings. An axis map converts user coordinates on an axis, such as weight 400, to the design coordinates of the masters. It is stored in the avar table and lets a slider feel even when masters are not. bottom sidebearing هامش سفلي proposed Derived from هامش جانبي; the word for side is dropped because the bearing is vertical. The space below the glyph outline within its vertical advance. This value participates in vertical text spacing rather than horizontal spacing. component مكون proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: مكون, plural مكونات. A component is a reference to another glyph placed inside this one, so that aacute holds the a and the acute rather than copies of their outlines. Change the source glyph and every glyph that references it follows. You build composites from components, position them with anchors, and keep them as references through to export, where a TrueType flavoured font stores them in the glyf table. In FontLab a component is one kind of element reference. composite glyph assembled glyph محرف مجمّع proposed Fallback 'assembled glyph' translated; the shadda disambiguates. Glyphs 3 Arabic and Font Book use مركب, rejected because حرف مركب is the ligature in Adobe and TS Fonts. A composite glyph is built from references to other glyphs rather than from its own outlines: an accented letter, a currency symbol with a bar, a stacked fraction. You assemble it from components and anchor them to the base, so a change to the base or to the mark reaches every composite that uses it. Composites keep a large accented character set consistent and small. A composite that has been decomposed is no longer one, and no longer follows its sources. conversion profile export settings set ملف تعريف التحويل proposed No attestation; ملف تعريف is the standard Arabic for a settings profile. Arabic uses تحويل for both conversion and transform. A conversion profile is the saved set of choices TransType applies to a conversion: the output format, the naming scheme, the filters, and the options that go with them. You build a profile once for a job you repeat, then run it over a new set of sources without repeating the decisions. It matters because a family converted with two different sets of options ships as two families that do not quite match, which shows up in a font menu rather than in a test. CVT table جدول CVT proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses جدول for font tables; the tag stays Latin. The CVT table holds the control values that TrueType hinting instructions refer to: the stem widths, heights, and other measurements a font wants held constant across glyphs. An instruction cites a CVT entry rather than a raw number, so one change to the table reaches every glyph that cites it. You work with it through the TrueType Hinting panel. It ships in the font, alongside the instructions themselves and the prep and fpgm programs that set the machine up. design space variation range فضاء التصميم proposed No attestation of the compound; فضاء is the mathematical word for a multi-dimensional space, where Glyphs 3 Arabic has مساحة الاستيفاء. A design space describes the positions defined by a font project's variation axes. Masters provide source data at specified locations; instances represent results at selected locations. User coordinates and internal design coordinates may be connected by a mapping, or may have the same values. State which coordinate system a number belongs to when the distinction affects a procedure. device correction per-size pixel correction تصحيح حسب الحجم proposed No attestation; fallback 'per-size pixel correction' translated, following the reviewed languages' size correction. A device correction adjusts a kerning or positioning value by whole pixels at one pixel size, to fix rounding at that size only. Stored in GPOS device tables; rarely needed on modern rasterizers. dimensions أبعاد proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic names its Dimensions panel لوحة الأبعاد. The font or family vertical values, such as ascender, descender, capital height, x-height and line gap. Distinguish these values from glyph spacing and canvas measurements. element عنصر proposed Standard Arabic UI word (Microsoft Visio, Krita); FontLab's element has no competing Arabic term. An element is FontLab's container for a piece of drawing inside a glyph: one or more contours, an image, or a reference to another element. A glyph holds elements, and an element holds contours, which is the layer of structure that makes a serif or a stem reusable across a family. You work with elements in the Elements panel and with the Element tool. The word is FontLab's own; other editors call the nearest thing a path group or a component. element reference shared drawing link مرجع عنصر proposed Derived from عنصر and مرجع; no attestation of the compound. An element reference is a placed copy of an element that still points at the original. Edit the original and every reference updates. You use references to share a serif, a stem, or a whole letter across a family, and you decompose a reference only when a glyph genuinely needs to diverge. A component is the familiar case of an element reference: one glyph placed inside another. Keep references intact through the design phase, since decomposing early throws away the link that makes a late change cheap. family dimensions أبعاد العائلة proposed Derived from أبعاد; عائلة is the standard Arabic for a font family. The vertical values used to establish line layout for a font family. Platform-specific ascender, descender and line-gap fields belong to this group. Flex Flex proposed Kept in Latin script as the PostScript operator name, as the reviewed languages do; Glyphs 3 Arabic transliterates فلكس. Flex is a PostScript hint that flattens a shallow curve, such as a cup serif, to a straight line at small sizes. FontLab marks glyphs that carry it. Keep the name. font dimensions أبعاد الخط proposed Derived from أبعاد and خط (font). The design dimensions of a font master, including ascender, descender, capital height and x-height. These values describe the vertical proportions of the design. font target export target خط الوجهة proposed No attestation; وجهة is the usual Arabic software word for a destination or target. A font target is what TransType produces from a source: the output font, with its format, its names, and the filters applied on the way. Sources go in on one side and targets come out on the other, and one source can produce several targets. You set the target options before you convert, and you name the target in a procedure step so a reader knows which side of the conversion a setting belongs to. font unit وحدة خط proposed Derived from Glyphs 3 Arabic الوحدات لكل Em; خط here means font. A font unit is the coordinate step of a font's design grid. UPM says how many of them make one em, so a 700 unit stem in a 1000 UPM font is 70 percent of the em. Metrics, kerning values and node coordinates are all stated in font units. fractional coordinates non-integer coordinates إحداثيات كسرية proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses إحداثيات for coordinates; كسري is the mathematical adjective. Fractional coordinates are node positions with decimal places, kept for curve fidelity while you draw. Font formats store integers, so FontLab rounds on export or when you turn on Round coordinates for the font. friendly glyph name readable glyph name اسم محرف مقروء proposed Fallback 'readable glyph name' translated; Glyphs 3 Arabic calls its nice names الأسماء اللطيفة. A friendly glyph name is the readable name FontLab shows for editing, such as Aacute, as opposed to the production name written into the exported font, such as uni00C1. FontLab can keep both and convert on export. ghost hint edge-only fitting instruction تلميح شبحي proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic has تلميح خيال for Ghost Hint; the adjective شبحي is the idiomatic form. A ghost hint is a PostScript hint with a special width that marks one edge, such as the top of a round letter, when there is no stem to hint. It aligns that edge to an alignment zone. hint screen fitting instruction تلميح proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: تلميح, plural تلميحات. Rejected the loan هنت/هنتنج. A hint is a stored instruction that tells a rasterizer how to align a stem or a zone to the pixel grid at small sizes. PostScript hints describe stems and zones; TrueType hints are instructions. FontLab draws hints in the Glyph window and generates them with autohinting. The word stays English in every language. hint zone hinting height band منطقة تلميح proposed Derived from تلميح and Glyphs 3 Arabic منطقة for zone. A hint zone is a horizontal band, such as the baseline or the x-height, inside which a rasterizer snaps overshoots to the same pixel row. FontLab stores zones in Font Info and shows them in the Glyph window. An alignment zone is the PostScript name for the same thing; hint zone is the general term. hinting screen fitting تلميح proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses the native تلميح, not the loan هنتنج; Arabic has one verbal noun for hint and hinting. Rejected TypeType's تحسين العرض. Hinting is the extra information a font carries so that its outlines land predictably on a pixel grid at small sizes. PostScript hinting declares stems and alignment zones and leaves the rasterizer to interpret them. TrueType hinting gives instructions that move points explicitly, with the control values in the CVT table. You work on PostScript hints in the glyph and in Font Info, and on TrueType hints with the TrueType Hinting tool and panel. Autohinting produces a starting point you then correct. instance generated design حالة proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses حالة consistently (أضف حالة, الحالة كماستر). Rejected نسخة and TypeType's descriptive الأنماط المولدة; a reviewer should confirm حالة does not read as 'state'. An instance is a particular result at a location in a font's variation space. A named instance, such as Semibold, gives a selected location a name that applications can present. Other locations need not have names. In FontLab, configured instances can be exported as static fonts or included as named instances in a variable font. interpolation استيفاء proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic and the TypeType glossary: الاستيفاء. Interpolation calculates values between source values. In font design, it can calculate outlines, metrics and other data from masters at specified design-space locations. Outline interpolation requires corresponding contour and point structures. Structural compatibility makes the calculation possible, but does not guarantee a good drawing: inspect intermediate results as well as the masters. Extrapolation calculates beyond the source range. kern exception pair spacing exception استثناء تقنين proposed No attestation; fallback translated and derived from تقنين. A kern exception is a pair value that overrides what the classes would otherwise apply. One member of a class rarely behaves like the rest, and the exception says so without breaking the class apart. You create one in the Kerning panel by kerning the single pair while its classes stay in place. Keep exceptions few: a class with many exceptions is the wrong class, and the cheaper fix is to split it rather than to list every disagreement. kerning pair spacing correction تقنين proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses التقنين and Adobe InDesign Arabic uses تقنين الأحرف; the native term wins over the loans كيرنينج/كيرنينغ (TypeType). The verb is قنّن; compounds take تقنين as second noun. Kerning adjusts the spacing of particular glyph combinations beyond their normal advances. A pair such as AV may need a different gap from the one produced by its unadjusted metrics. OpenType fonts commonly store horizontal kerning in GPOS lookups associated with the kern feature; some formats and workflows use a separate kern table. Name the mechanism when it matters to export or compatibility. kerning class pair spacing group فئة تقنين proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: فئة التقنين اليسرى/اليمنى. Derived from تقنين; مجموعة تقنين is kept for kerning group. A kerning class groups glyphs that need the same kerning. You put every glyph that behaves alike on one side into one class, then kern the class once instead of kerning each pair inside it. FontLab applies the class value to every member pair and keeps single pairs as exceptions where a member needs its own value. Classes matter because a text face carries thousands of readable pairs, and a hand kerned list of that size is unmaintainable. FontLab writes the result into GPOS as class based positioning. kerning pair spacing-corrected pair زوج تقنين proposed Derived from تقنين; Adobe InDesign Arabic help calls the pairs أزواج. No direct attestation of the compound. A kerning pair associates two glyphs, or two kerning classes, with a spacing adjustment. In horizontal kerning, a negative value normally reduces the gap and a positive value increases it. An individual glyph pair may provide an exception to class kerning, but it can also exist without a class rule. Check pairs in representative text as well as in isolation. left sidebearing هامش جانبي أيسر proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: الهامش الجانبي الأيسر. Keep numeric controls compact: LSB/RSB (French AG/AD), UPM and PPM. Expanded terms belong in explanatory help; the full Family Dimensions Units Per eM label is an intentional exception. Team UI convention in Proteus 1751b28b0. The horizontal space between the glyph origin and the left edge of its outline. It contributes to the glyph advance width and its spacing. Lib Lib proposed Kept in Latin script: it mirrors the UFO lib key, as the reviewed languages do. Lib is the custom metadata dictionary of a font or a master, mirroring the UFO lib and stored in VFJ. Scripts and tools keep their own keys there. line gap فجوة السطر proposed No attestation; literal and short, with سطر for a line of text so it is not read as خط (font). The line gap is extra vertical space between lines that a font recommends beyond ascender and descender. hhea and OS/2 each store one. line height ارتفاع السطر proposed Standard Arabic rendering of line height in web and layout software. The distance between successive text baselines. It includes the relevant ascender, descender and line-gap contributions; line gap alone is only the additional space. link metrics tie spacing to another glyph ربط المقاييس proposed Derived from مقاييس; no attestation of the command. Link metrics ties a glyph's sidebearing or advance width to another glyph or to an expression, so the value follows its source. FontLab shows linked metrics with the expression and updates them when the source changes. linked metrics مقاييس مرتبطة proposed Derived from مقاييس and ربط. Glyph spacing values linked to another glyph or to an expression. Updating the source or expression changes the dependent advance width or sidebearings. mark attachment combining mark positioning تموضع العلامات proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: تموضع/موضعة العلامات for mark positioning, which is what the fallback names. Mark attachment positions a combining mark relative to a base glyph, a ligature component or another mark. OpenType GPOS lookups describe the anchor relationships, and the shaping engine applies the positioning during layout. FontLab can generate attachment code from suitable anchors. Check the relevant generation settings and test combinations, including stacked marks, rather than assuming that every anchor automatically becomes a lookup. master source design ماستر proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses the loan ماستر consistently (أضف ماستر, توافق الماستر); an attested professional loan. Plural ماسترات. Rejected رئيسي (office-suite slide master) and TypeType's descriptive الأنماط الأساسية. A master provides source outlines and other font data at a specified location in a design space. Masters can describe weight, width or other variations, including intermediate locations. FontLab uses corresponding data from masters to calculate instances. For outline interpolation, check contour and point compatibility in each affected glyph; the word master alone does not guarantee that every glyph is present or compatible. master compatibility matching master structure توافق الماسترات proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: توافق الماستر; plural used here because the condition holds between masters. Master compatibility is the condition every glyph must meet before it can interpolate: the same number of contours in the same order, with the same number of nodes and the same start point in each. FontLab reports incompatible glyphs and gives you Matchmaker to repair them by matching contours and start points between masters. Fix compatibility before you tune shapes, because a repair that reorders nodes moves every curve that depends on them. metrics مقاييس proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: المقاييس. قياسات (TypeType, Font Book) is kept for canvas measurements. Metrics are the measurements that place a glyph in a line: its advance width and its two sidebearings. Vertical metrics are a separate set, the font wide values for ascender, descender, and line gap. You work on horizontal metrics in the Metrics panel and with the Metrics tool, and on vertical metrics in Font Info. Say which set you mean whenever a page discusses both, because a reader who applies a horizontal instruction to the vertical fields breaks line spacing everywhere the font is used. metrics expression تعبير مقاييس proposed Derived from مقاييس; تعبير is the standard Arabic for an expression. An expression that calculates a glyph advance width or sidebearing from other values. It describes a spacing relationship rather than a canvas measurement. metrics key مفتاح مقاييس proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: مفاتيح المقاييس. A glyph reference or expression used to derive a spacing value. The referenced value determines an advance width or sidebearing. pin دبوس proposed Issue 160 catalog family review: named point inside an element, distinct from a glyph-layer anchor. Proteus Resources/helptips.json def.anchorpin defines the behavior. Preserve this term across panel, tool, action and help labels; proposed terminology, not native-team approval. A pin is a named point inside an element. Use pins to position elements with expressions and to attach elements to each other. An anchor is a named point in a glyph layer, used for component placement and mark attachment. Create either with the Guides tool and edit it in the Anchors and Pins panel. PPM pixels per type body بكسل لكل em proposed Built on the UPM pattern; no attestation. The abbreviation PPM stays Latin in compact hinting fields. Keep numeric controls compact: LSB/RSB (French AG/AD), UPM and PPM. Expanded terms belong in explanatory help; the full Family Dimensions Units Per eM label is an intentional exception. Team UI convention in Proteus 1751b28b0. PPM, pixels per em, is the size at which a rasterizer renders a font: how many pixels one em occupies. TrueType hints, device corrections and bitmap strikes are specified per PPM. In explanatory prose expand it; in hinting fields the short form is usual. production glyph name shipping glyph name اسم إنتاج المحرف proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: اسم الإنتاج, with محرف added as the English does. A production glyph name is the name written into the exported font, chosen for compatibility with tools and the Adobe Glyph List, such as uni00C1 rather than Aacute. rendering drawing on screen تصيير proposed GIMP and Scribus Arabic use تصيير; rejected تظهير (Khalid Alabdullah's blog) as less widespread. Rendering is the conversion of an outline into pixels on a screen or a printer. The rasterizer of the operating system or of FontLab's preview reads the outline, applies the hints and paints the result. FontLab previews rendering at chosen pixel sizes so you can judge hints. Rasterization names the same step from the pixel side. required glyphs mandatory glyphs محارف إلزامية proposed No attestation; fallback 'mandatory glyphs' translated. Required glyphs are the ones the OpenType specification and common tools expect at the start of a font: .notdef, NULL or uni0000, CR or uni000D and space. FontLab can add them on export. right sidebearing هامش جانبي أيمن proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: الهامش الجانبي الأيمن. Keep numeric controls compact: LSB/RSB (French AG/AD), UPM and PPM. Expanded terms belong in explanatory help; the full Family Dimensions Units Per eM label is an intentional exception. Team UI convention in Proteus 1751b28b0. The horizontal space between the right edge of a glyph outline and the end of its advance width. It contributes to spacing. sidebearing side space هامش جانبي proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: الهامش الجانبي الأيسر/الأيمن. Rejected TypeType's فراغ جانبي and TS Fonts' مسافات جانبية in favour of the font-editor term. A sidebearing is the space between a glyph's outline and the edge of its advance width: the left sidebearing before the shape, the right sidebearing after it. Together with the advance width it sets how the glyph spaces against every other glyph, which is the work that carries a text face further than kerning does. You edit sidebearings in the Metrics panel or with the Metrics tool, one glyph at a time or across a selection, and you check them in a word rather than in isolation. size حجم proposed Standard Arabic for size in Apple, Adobe and Glyphs (حجم الخط). The size of an object or the chosen size of displayed text. Name a specific width or height when only one direction is intended. spacing تباعد proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic, Apple CoreText and the TypeType glossary all use التباعد. The adjustment of glyph advance widths and sidebearings to establish the space between letters. Kerning makes additional adjustments to particular pairs. standard stem reference stem width ساق قياسية proposed Derived from ساق; no attestation of the compound. Standard stems are the representative horizontal and vertical stem widths declared in a font for hinting. The rasterizer snaps stems near those widths to the same pixel count, so like stems stay alike at small sizes. stem link stem tie رابط ساق proposed No attestation; fallback 'stem tie' translated and derived from ساق. A stem link ties two edges of a stroke together as a stem, so hinting can hold their distance as the size changes. A vertical link governs a horizontal measurement and a horizontal link governs a vertical one. You add links in the glyph, either by hand or from an autohinting pass, and you keep them consistent with the standard stem widths declared in Font Info. Vextra reuses the term for the paired edges it detects in artwork that is not type. styling group name اسم مجموعة الأنماط proposed No attestation; built on مجموعة and نمط, Apple's word for a font style. The styling group name, SGN, ties together the styles an application reaches through its bold and italic buttons, and the styling link value and styling link name say which slot each style takes in that group. The mechanism is older than typographic family names and narrower: four slots, no more. You set these fields in TransType when a family has to behave correctly in applications that still drive style selection from those buttons. subsetting cutting down a font إنشاء مجموعة فرعية proposed Apple Font Book: إنشاء مجموعة فرعية من الخط. Subsetting exports only part of a font, such as the glyphs a page uses or one codepage, to make a smaller file. The OS/2 embedding bits can forbid it. top sidebearing هامش علوي proposed Derived from هامش جانبي; the word for side is dropped because the bearing is vertical. The space above the glyph outline within its vertical advance. This value participates in vertical text spacing rather than horizontal spacing. tracking uniform letter spacing تتبع proposed Adobe InDesign Arabic help pairs تقنين الأحرف with التتبع, and تتبع is the most frequent rendering in the corpus. Rejected the older InDesign label ضبط تجانب الحروف as long and opaque. Tracking changes the spacing across a run of text, rather than correcting particular pairs as kerning does. Layout applications apply it to text. TransType's Tracking filter changes spacing in the font data itself. That changes the font's starting metrics; a layout application can still apply additional tracking to text set in the resulting font. TrueType instruction pixel fitting instruction تعليمة TrueType proposed تعليمة is the standard Arabic for a program instruction; no attestation of the compound. A TrueType instruction is one step of the program a TrueType font runs to fit an outline to the pixel grid. Instructions are the TrueType form of hints. FontLab writes them from visual TrueType hints and can keep the ones a font already has. Say instruction for the code and hint for what the reader draws. typographic family name اسم العائلة الطباعي proposed Apple CoreText uses طباعي for typographic; عائلة for family. The typographic family name, TFN, is the name that groups every style of a family under one entry, and the typographic style name, TSN, is what distinguishes a style inside it. They sit beside the older four style family and style names that legacy applications read. You set them in TransType and in Font Info, and you keep them consistent across a family, because an app that reads these fields builds its font menu from them. update metrics تحديث المقاييس proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: تحديث for Update and المقاييس for metrics. Recalculate glyph spacing values from their links or expressions. This command updates the advance widths and sidebearings that depend on those relationships. variable font خط متغير proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic and TS Fonts: الخط المتغير, الخطوط المتغيرة. A variable font contains data for design variation along one or more axes. Applications select axis values and calculate the corresponding outlines and other variable data. Named instances identify selected locations, but users are not limited to those locations when the application exposes axis controls. A variable font's supported range depends on its data; it need not contain every style in the family. variation location position in the variation range موضع proposed Follows the reviewed languages, which say only position; Apple CoreText uses موضع for position. A variation location is a point in the design space, given as one value per axis. Masters and instances each have one, and the Variations panel slider shows the current one. vertical advance glyph box height تقدم رأسي proposed Same concept as advance height, so the same term; no attestation, fallback translated. The vertical advance is the distance a glyph advances in vertical text, the counterpart of advance width for East Asian layout. Stored in vmtx. vertical metrics مقاييس رأسية proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: المقاييس الرأسية. The font-wide vertical values used for line layout, including ascender, descender and line gap. FontLab groups these as dimensions, distinct from glyph spacing metrics. visual kerning shape-measured spacing correction تقنين بصري proposed Adobe InDesign Arabic calls optical kerning تقنين الأحرف البصري; derived from تقنين. Visual kerning is kerning that FontLab proposes by measuring the shapes, so that a font gets a usable first pass without a person typing thousands of values. You run it over a selection, then review what it produced, because a measurement of two outlines does not know about the words a reader will meet. Treat the result as a draft: keep the pairs it got right, correct the ones it did not, and kern the difficult pairs by eye in real words. weight axis thickness axis محور الوزن proposed Derived from محور and وزن; TS Fonts names the weight axis this way. The weight axis, tag wght, varies stroke thickness from light to bold. In a variable font it is the most common axis; its master locations use the usWeightClass scale, such as 400 for Regular and 700 for Bold. weight class فئة الوزن proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: فئة الوزن. The weight class is the OS/2 value from 100 to 900 that tells applications how heavy a style is, with 400 for Regular and 700 for Bold. Style linking and menus rely on it. width axis narrow-to-wide axis محور العرض proposed Derived from محور and عرض. The width axis, tag wdth, varies letter proportions from condensed to extended. It is distinct from advance width, which is the spacing of one glyph, and from the geometric width of a shape. Its scale is a percentage of normal width. width class فئة العرض proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: فئة العرض. The width class is the OS/2 value from 1, ultra condensed, to 9, ultra expanded, that tells applications how wide a style is. It is a classification, not the width axis value and not the advance width.

docs.title: OpenType
docs.text: English Fallback Arabic Status Note Definition Adobe Glyph List Adobe Glyph List do-not-translate The Adobe Glyph List maps standard glyph names to Unicode codepoints, so that a glyph named aacute is understood as U plus 00E1 by any tool that follows it. You name glyphs by it wherever it covers the character, because tools and text engines can then infer the mapping without being told twice. Where it does not cover a glyph, you fall back to a consistent scheme of your own and assign codepoints explicitly. Write the name in full on first mention, then AGL. alternate glyph glyph variant محرف بديل proposed Derived from محرف and بديل. An alternate glyph is another form of the same character, selected through an OpenType feature such as salt or a stylistic set. Its name usually carries a suffix, as in a.alt or g.ss01. cmap cmap do-not-translate The cmap table maps character codes to glyph indices. Its Unicode subtables provide the initial mapping used in text rendering; other subtables support particular encodings or variation sequences. FontLab generates these mappings from the project's encoding data. A glyph without its own Unicode assignment can still appear in typed text through substitution, such as a ligature or alternate selected by the shaping engine. code page legacy character table صفحة ترميز proposed Microsoft Arabic: صفحة الترميز. A code page is a numbered legacy encoding, such as Windows 1250 for Central European languages, that maps one byte to one character. The OS/2 table lists the code pages a font supports, and FontLab derives that list from the glyphs present. Write two words. color font table جدول خط ملون proposed Derived from جدول and Font Book's ملون for colour glyphs. Colour-font tables store data for colour glyph rendering. Formats include COLR with CPAL, SVG, sbix, and CBDT with CBLC. They differ in how they describe vector or bitmap content and in application support. Including several formats can extend coverage, but does not guarantee rendering in every application. Identify the exported formats and test the intended targets. contextual alternates context-dependent variants بدائل سياقية proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic, Adobe InDesign Arabic and TS Fonts all use البدائل السياقية. Contextual alternates, the calt feature, cover substitutions an app makes because of what sits around a glyph rather than because a reader asked. In a script face the text engine replaces an entry stroke after a letter that already ends in one, and in a face with repeating shapes it replaces the second of a pair. You write the rules with context in feature code, and apps usually leave calt on by default, which makes it the feature most likely to surprise you when a rule is too broad. cursive attachment joined-script connection تموضع متصل proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: تموضع متصل for cursive positioning. Cursive attachment joins glyphs by matching an exit anchor of one glyph to the entry anchor of the next, so connected scripts such as Arabic and Nastaliq flow. It is the curs feature, built from anchors. design languages لغات مستهدفة proposed No attestation; follows the reviewed languages (target languages), because لغات التصميم reads as visual design languages. Design languages, the meta table dlng record, list the languages the typeface was designed for. Supported languages, slng, list every language it can set. Both are language tags, not feature tags. encoding ترميز proposed Apple, Microsoft and the TypeType glossary use ترميز. An encoding maps character codes to glyphs. Unicode is the encoding modern fonts use; legacy encodings such as Mac Roman or a code page map one byte to one glyph. FontLab shows the font in a chosen encoding in the Font window and writes the cmap from it. Say encoding for the mapping and code page for a numbered legacy table. feature code layout rule code كود الميزات proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: كود الميزة. Feature code is the text syntax that describes OpenType features: classes, lookups, substitution and positioning rules, grouped into features by tag. It is usually called FEA, after the file extension. You edit it in the Features panel, compile it to check for errors, and keep it under the same review as the drawings, since a rule that fires on the wrong glyph is as visible as a wrong outline. FontLab compiles it into GSUB and GPOS at export. fractions كسور proposed Apple CoreText and Glyphs: كسور. Fractions are numerical forms such as ½. In OpenType, the frac feature supports diagonal fraction composition through glyph substitution. A font may provide precomposed fraction glyphs, numerator and denominator forms, or both. The separate numr and dnom features provide numerator and denominator forms. Do not substitute the sups and subs feature names for these mechanisms or promise support for every input sequence without testing it. glyph index glyph number فهرس المحرف proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic uses فهارس for indexes; rejected Font Book's مؤشر, which means pointer. A glyph index is the number a glyph occupies in the font's own order, counting from zero. Text engines work in indices after the cmap has done its job, and binary tables reference glyphs by index rather than by name. You rarely set one by hand, but you meet it when you inspect a compiled font or debug a lookup that fires on the wrong glyph. The index depends on glyph order, so it changes when the order does. glyph name اسم المحرف proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: اسم المحرف. A glyph name identifies a glyph in an editing project, feature code or a tool's data. Names such as a, a.sc and a.alt can distinguish related drawings. They are separate from Unicode assignments and glyph indices, and need not survive in every exported format. After renaming a glyph, check references in feature code, classes and scripts, including references the editor cannot update automatically. GPOS GPOS do-not-translate GPOS is the OpenType table that holds positioning: kerning, mark attachment, cursive attachment, and any rule that moves a glyph without replacing it. FontLab writes your kerning here, as pairs and as class based positioning, and builds the mark lookups from your anchors. You reach it through feature code rather than by editing the table. A font may also carry a legacy kern table; modern text engines read GPOS and many ignore the other. GSUB GSUB do-not-translate GSUB is the OpenType table containing glyph-substitution lookups. It supports operations such as replacing a glyph with an alternate, forming a ligature or selecting a form from its context. FontLab compiles feature code into these structures. To diagnose a missing substitution, check the glyphs, compiled rules, feature selection, language and shaping order in the target application. ligature joined letters حرف مركب proposed Adobe Arabic (الحروف المركبة), TS Fonts (المركبات) and Glyphs 3 Arabic (مركبة). Rejected Apple's أحرف متصلة, because all Arabic letters join, and TypeType's الرابطة. A ligature is a glyph used to represent a sequence of characters, such as fi. OpenType substitution can replace several glyphs with one ligature glyph. The liga and dlig features distinguish standard and discretionary ligatures. Shaping does not change the underlying text; whether a later document export preserves searchable text also depends on that export and its text mappings. localized forms language-specific variants أشكال محلية proposed Glyphs 3 Arabic: أشكال محلية. Localized forms are glyph variants selected for a text run's language. The OpenType locl feature can provide these substitutions, for example Bulgarian forms of Cyrillic letters. The shaping engine needs the relevant language information, which the application may obtain from a setting or other context. The substitution changes glyph selection, not the underlying characters or their codepoints. lookup procedure إجراء proposed User/team procedure fallback. No sufficiently strong established OpenType-specific alternative verified in the reviewed primary sources. Keep the approved contextual Rules panel title. Preserve literal FEA lookup/lookupflag keywords, identifiers and OpenType structure names. Ordinary search senses are separate. A lookup groups substitution or positioning rules of one type in GSUB or GPOS. Features reference lookups, and several features can share one.
